question.text: Overconfidence bias in investing leads to:

answer.text: Excessive trading, concentrated positions, and underestimation of risk based on overestimating one's ability to pick stocks

explanation.text: The Logic: Overconfidence bias, in behavioural-finance research, is the tendency of investors to overestimate their stock-picking and market-timing ability. Empirically, it manifests as (a) excessive trading, which drives up transaction costs and tax drag, (b) concentrated portfolios that lack diversification because the investor "knows" which positions will win, and (c) underestimation of downside risk because outcomes are attributed to skill rather than to chance. By definition, overconfidence does not produce more diversification, better risk management, or more conservative choices — the bias works in the opposite direction. The Trap: Distractors describe the prudent behaviours one would expect from a self-aware investor; overconfident investors do the opposite. Note: The specific claim that overconfidence causes excessive trading, concentrated positions and underestimation of risk is not stated on the NISM Series XV Research Analyst workbook pages checked (which cover loss-aversion, confirmation, ownership, gambler's fallacy, winner's curse, herd mentality, anchoring and projection, and only mention overconfidence in passing); the framing above reflects the standard behavioural-finance literature on overconfidence rather than a workbook citation.
